Design Block on New Data

Source: R/generics.R
term_predict.Rd

Applies a built term's recorded mapping to new rows, returning the block that the term would have produced had those rows been in the data on which it was built. Factor levels, contrasts, spline knots and a Demmler-Reinsch reparametrization come from the blueprint and are reused; the spreads of a standardization enter the penalty only and are not applied to the block. A factor level that the blueprint does not contain is rejected, except for the grouping levels of a random() term with unseen = "zero".

Usage

term_predict(term, newdata, ...)

Arguments

term

A built additive term (see term_build()). A specification signals the error "the term has not been built; call term_build(term, data) first.".

newdata

A data frame carrying every variable that the term names, with any number of rows. Any other object is rejected by the generic, before dispatch, with the error "'newdata' must be a data frame.". A factor here need carry only the levels that its own rows use; the rest come from the blueprint.

...

Passed to methods. The method for random() reads unseen. Its default "error" rejects a grouping level that was absent at the build and a missing grouping value; with unseen = "zero" such a row receives a row of zeros. The other shipped methods do not use it.

Value

A block of nrow(newdata) rows and term_npar() columns, in the same storage that the term built: a numeric matrix, or a Matrix object where the block is sparse.

The identity that makes it useful

The block returned is \(\tilde{X}_t\) such that \(\tilde{\eta} = \tilde{X}_t \beta_t\) is the term's contribution at the new rows, at the coefficients that the model already carries. The identity holds because the mapping is reused. A rebuilt encoding gives a block of the same shape that multiplies the same coefficients but means something else: a factor whose new rows omit a level loses a column, and a basis rebuilt on a narrower range is a different set of functions.

For a smooth, predicting on a subset of the fitting rows reproduces the corresponding rows of the original block exactly, whereas rebuilding the term on the subset gives a block that multiplies the coefficients by different functions. The subset check of check_term() makes this comparison.

Predicting on the fitting data returns the block itself, so term_predict(b, data) and term_matrix(b) agree to the last bit.

Which terms have a method

The methods are registered for linpar(), the penalized terms, random(), the smooths, nl() and the break-point terms. A structural term contributes no block and has no method, so term_predict() on one signals S7's method-not-found error; term_continue() is the corresponding operation there.

See also

term_matrix() for the block on the fitting data, term_build() for what records the blueprint, check_term() for the check that takes this identity as its subject, and term_continue() for a structural term.

Examples

d <- data.frame(x = 1:6, g = factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c"), 2)))
b <- term_build(linpar(~ x + g), d)

# New rows go through the same mapping as the fitting rows.
term_predict(b, data.frame(x = c(0.5, 2.5), g = factor(c("a", "c"))))
#>   (Intercept)   x gb gc
#> 1           1 0.5  0  0
#> 2           1 2.5  0  1

# On the fitting data it returns the block itself.
all.equal(term_predict(b, d), term_matrix(b))
#> [1] TRUE

# A subset that drops a level keeps the blueprint's columns, where a
# rebuild would lose one.
nd <- droplevels(d[d$g != "c", ])
dim(term_predict(b, nd))
#> [1] 4 4
dim(model.matrix(~ x + g, nd))
#> [1] 4 3

# A basis is not replaced on the narrower range: reapplying agrees with
# the original rows exactly, rebuilding does not.
d2  <- data.frame(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 60))
bs  <- term_build(s(x, basis7::bspline_smooth(k = 6)), d2)
X   <- term_matrix(bs)
sub <- 1:20
max(abs(term_predict(bs, d2[sub, , drop = FALSE]) - X[sub, ]))
#> [1] 0
max(abs(term_matrix(term_build(s(x, basis7::bspline_smooth(k = 6)), d2[sub, , drop = FALSE])) -
        X[sub, ]))
#> [1] 2.331092
